newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan markets seen volatile after Bhutto ouster.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan markets seen volatile after Bhutto ouster.

text.p: Pakistan's financial markets seem set for a period of volatility and uncertainty as caution sets in following the dismissal of Benazir Bhutto's government, analysts said on Tuesday.
"We expect the market to remain volatile during November and December with a trading band between 1,430 and 1,550 points," Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring, told Reuters.

The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index, which soared 78 points in a celebratory response to Bhutto's removal, has slipped in several sessions since. It regained some ground on Tuesday to close 6.71 points higher at 1,486.21.

"With investors still licking the wounds of last week's market volatility, we believe that they will be more cautious in their reaction towards new developments," Nadeem Naqvi, head of research at Taurus Securities, said.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto on charges of corruption and misrule a week ago and installed an interim government to supervise elections set for February 3.

The market's euphoria over the dismissal was short-lived. A cut in Pakistan's credit ratings by Moody's Investors Services Inc sent the index down 70 points on November 7, only a day after the market's initial 78-point leap.
Dealers said recent select buying in blue chips has offset earlier speculative selling, but overall sentiment remains weak.
Analysts welcomed plans by the new caretaker government to reform state-run banks and financial institutions, but said lack of clear details had kept the market guessing.

"The new government has yet to clarify its plan of action and whatever plans we have heard are likely to be extremely difficult to implement given the short three-month period at its disposal," KAB Securities analyst Faisal Abbas Bhayani said.

In the currency market, dealers said the uncertain outlook meant speculators dominated trading. The rupee opened 0.05 rupee up at 42.65 to the dollar in the kerb market, but dealers said it might fall before the close.
"Unless clarity emerges regarding the monetary and fiscal policy of the caretaker government the market will continue to see-saw," dealer Owais Kalia said.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan rate was unchanged at 40.1200/40.3206 to the dollar set on October 22.
Bankers said the rupee could stay under pressure given a shortage of dollars in the interbank market due to a widening trade deficit, low foreign reserves and rising inflation.
"The market perception is that the rupee may depreciate by at least five to seven percent before the end of December," forex analyst Fahim Ahmad at Banque Indosuez said.

The central bank said last week that foreign reserves, including bullion and special drawing rights, stood at $1.262 billion, on October 31, down from $1.865 billion in September and $1.963 billion in October 1995.
Ahmad said the dollar-starved interbank forex market had been lifting an average of $20 million to $25 million daily from the central bank for the last couple of weeks.
He also said six-month forward dollars were currently being offered at a premium of 0.61 rupee above the official rate. A few months ago the premium was only 0.25 rupee.
"The alarming trade deficit figure released yesterday signals that the six-month premium would be range-bound at the 0.60- to 0.65-rupee levels," he said.
The trade deficit rose to a provisional $443 million in October from $264 million in September and $415 million in October 1995, the Federal Bureau of Statistics said on Monday.
